text: Capability classes. A way to predict where effects pay off, before you write a handler.
Every handler is classified by one question: what does it demand of k, the rest of the program?
Four classes. Each contains the one before, and each step up buys power, at a cost.
Class zero, dispatch. The handler performs the operation, and resumes k once, right away.
The same program runs under a handler that routes to a provider, or under a test handler.
This is the runtime power of dependency injection. A function call would do.
Class one, data middleware. k is still resumed once, but the handler works around that one resume.
memo reads the effect as data. A repeated question is answered from its cache, without a call.
retry yields the effect again for each attempt. Two attempts fail, and the third one answers.
Then it resumes k once, with the first success. Retrying the operation is class one.
Inspect, accumulate, elide, transform, repeat: around one resume, all of them can be built.
Class two, scheduling. Here k escapes the handler. It is parked, and resumed later.
Task one asks for prices. The backend call takes two seconds, on a virtual clock.
Half a second later, task two asks for the same prices. The dedup handler parks its k.
When the call returns, both tasks resume with the same value. Two calls served three requests.
Dependency injection has no continuations, so it cannot reach this class.
Class three, multi-shot, is deliberately absent. Every k in doeff is one-shot.
A handler that resumes k a second time gets a runtime error.
The sanctioned approximation: run the whole program again, once per branch, with a memoized prefix.
Both branches run, and the expensive call before the branch point happens only once.
When does adopting effects pay? One rule explains the audited projects.
First, you need to change what call boundaries do, at composition time or at run time.
Second, the call behind a boundary must cost far more than intercepting it.
One effect cost three and a half microseconds. Next to a ten millisecond call, that is 0.03 percent.
In a hot loop, it is forty-nine times a plain step. Keep such loops below the effect boundary.
Ask what a handler does with k. It tells you the cost, and whether you need effects at all.
